dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Welcome to WKU Radio. Today we're asking students to describe a place that matters to them. First, we have Daniyar. Daniyar, tell us about your place.

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: My place is a small café in Aktobe — the city where I grew up. It's a place that I've been going to since I was about twelve years old.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Can you describe it for us?

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: It's a café which my grandmother used to take me to every Saturday. It's a small, slightly old-fashioned place that serves traditional Kazakh food. The walls are covered in old photographs which show Aktobe in the 1970s and 80s.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: What makes it special for you?

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: It's the people who run it. An elderly couple who have worked there for decades. They know everyone by name. It's a place where you always feel recognised — like you matter to someone.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Has it changed much since you were young?

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: Very little. The chairs are the same ones that were there when I was a child. The menu, which hasn't changed since the 1990s, still has the same soup that my grandmother always ordered.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Thank you. Next is Kamila. Kamila, what's your place?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Mine is actually a library — not WKU, but the public library in Almaty where I used to go as a teenager. It's a large, beautiful building that was built in the Soviet era.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: What do you remember most about it?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: The silence. And the smell. And the feeling that you were surrounded by ideas that someone had cared about enough to write down. It's a place that made me want to become the kind of person who also cared about ideas.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Beautiful. Do you still go there?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Every time I'm in Almaty. I sit in the same reading room where I used to study for exams. It's become a place that connects me to who I was at sixteen.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Thank you both. You've described places that clearly define who you are.

questions.text: "It's a café which my grandmother used to take me to." "Which" refers to:
questions.hint: "which" = relative pronoun for things. The café is a thing → use "which" (or "that"). ✅

questions.text: "The people who run it." — "who" is used because:
questions.hint: "who" = relative pronoun for people. "The people WHO run it." ✅

questions.text: "The menu, which hasn't changed since the 1990s, still has the same soup." — "which" refers to:
questions.hint: "which" refers back to the nearest noun: "the menu." A thing → "which." ✅

questions.text: "It's a place ___ you always feel recognised."
questions.hint: "where" = relative pronoun for places. "A place WHERE you feel recognised." ✅

questions.text: "A large, beautiful building that was built..." — "that" refers to:
questions.hint: "that" can replace "which" for things. "A building THAT was built in the Soviet era." ✅

questions.text: "Photographs which show Aktobe." Which pronoun can also replace "which" here?
questions.hint: For things: "which" and "that" are both correct. "Photographs THAT show Aktobe." ✅

questions.text: "An elderly couple ___ have worked there for decades."
questions.hint: "who" = people. "An elderly couple WHO have worked there for decades." ✅

questions.text: Which relative pronoun completes: "A place ___ I feel at home."?
questions.hint: "where" for places. "A place WHERE I feel at home." ✅ (You could also say "a place that makes me feel at home" — different structure)
